item.title: Bridging Perceptual and Value Signal Evaluation: Meta‐Analytic Evidence for the Claustrum as a Cross‐Domain Integrator in Decision‐Making
item.author: Yumin Liu, Geng Li, Yafen Li, Jialiang Chen, Huiyu Shi, Antao Chen
item.content:encoded: Across 90 fMRI studies, ALE and MACM reveal partly specialized fronto-parietal–visual and striato-thalamo-cingulate systems for perceptual and value signal evaluation. Shared convergence in the bilateral claustrum and left medial frontal gyrus highlights candidate cross-domain coordination nodes in decision-making.Decision-making requires evaluating information across both perceptual and value domains, yet the neural mechanisms supporting this cross-domain convergence remain unclear. Using activation likelihood estimation (ALE) and meta-analytic connectivity modeling (MACM), we conducted a large-scale cross-domain meta-analysis of 90 fMRI studies involving 2564 participants to examine the neural correlates of perceptual and value signal evaluation. The results revealed partially segregated yet overlapping neural architectures for perceptual and value signal evaluation. Perceptual signal evaluation was primarily associated with a dorsal fronto-parietal–visual system, whereas value signal evaluation was mainly associated with a striato-thalamo-cingulate system. Importantly, the conjunction analysis identified the bilateral claustrum and left medial frontal gyrus as shared convergence regions across domains. MACM further showed distinguishable coactivation profiles, suggesting that these shared regions may participate in coordinating domain-specific perceptual and value-related networks rather than forming a single common decision system. Together, these findings support the claustrum as a candidate domain-general integrator that may bridge sensory, motivational, and executive processes, providing a cross-domain account of decision-making.

item.title: Harmonization of Longitudinal Multi‐Scanner Neuroimaging Data With Nonlinear Biological Associations
item.author: Neel M. Desai, Haochang Shou, Noah Hillman, Randa Melhem, Lori L. Beason‐Held, Susan M. Resnick, Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging, Christos Davatzikos, Russell T. Shinohara
item.content:encoded: We develop a ComBat-based approach to harmonize longitudinal multi-source imaging data that can flexibly account for non-linear biological associations of interest. Our method outperforms existing ComBat-based harmonization approaches designed for longitudinal data.The aggregation of neuroimaging data across multiple sources, typically scanners or imaging sites, has the potential to improve statistical power when conducting inference. The added benefits of increased sample size to inference, however, can be obstructed by unwanted source-specific technical variability that increases difficulty in estimating biological signals of interest. To address this issue, recent methods based on ComBat, a batch-correction procedure originally developed for genomics, have been developed for both cross-sectional and longitudinal neuroimaging data. While these approaches have successfully removed technical batch-specific variability, they restrict their consideration to linear biological associations. In this article we introduce a ComBat-based method to harmonize longitudinal multisource imaging data that can account for nonlinear biological associations of interest. We demonstrate via simulation that, in the presence of nonlinear biological signal, our method outperforms existing ComBat-based approaches designed for longitudinal imaging data, particularly in settings where observed values of relevant biological covariates lack substantial overlap across sources. Using volumetric measurements for 504 subjects combined from both the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging (BLSA) and the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI), we identify the presence of both additive and multiplicative study-specific effects for a substantial number of brain regions and demonstrate the effective removal of their presence on data harmonized by our method. The flexibility of the proposed method towards capturing many types of biological associations makes it a versatile procedure that can be used to harmonize longitudinal biomedical data.

item.title: Interdependent conditions for successful human–AI delegation
item.author: Felipe M. Affonso, Mark Steyvers
item.content:encoded: People increasingly rely on AI systems for consequential tasks, from clinical diagnosis to software development. The gains are real yet difficult to realize reliably. We identify four psychological and structural conditions for successful delegation: accurate human assessment of AI capabilities, calibrated AI uncertainty communication, sustained human monitoring capacity, and compatible task structure. Each condition is well-studied, yet we propose that they form an interdependent system in which each one’s effectiveness depends on the state of the others. Because these dependencies are bidirectional, we suggest that they can compound over time into virtuous cycles or cascading degradation, and that improving any single condition can fail or shift the bottleneck. These dynamics should intensify as AI moves from advisory roles to autonomous agents.

item.title: The neuroscience of delirium: a perfect storm for acute brain dysfunction
item.author: Eyal Kimchi
item.content:encoded: Delirium is a highly prevalent, but much neglected, acute neuropsychiatric syndrome strongly associated with dementia. In this Review, Cunningham and Kimchi detail the neurophysiological and neuroanatomical basis of delirium and the metabolic and neuroinflammatory mechanisms that may drive it.

item.title: The many facets of human brain asymmetry
item.author: Clyde Francks
item.content:encoded: Contrasting the right and left hemisphere has undergone a methodological and conceptual transformation. In this Review, Francks and colleagues focus on brain asymmetry as a multivariate and multiscale organizational feature of the human brain while discussing its variability across individuals and how left–right asymmetry supports cognition and behaviour.

item.title: Loss of confidence in commercial antibody validation threatens biomedical research integrity
item.author: Theam Soon Lim
item.content:encoded: Recent independent investigations conducted have identified thousands of apparently manipulated validation images across the online catalogues of more than a dozen commercial antibody suppliers. This points to a problem embedded in the antibody supply chain rather than at any single company. This represents a previously unaddressed entry point for unreliable data into biomedical research, upstream of the peer-review and image-integrity safeguards journals have put in place for manuscripts. This revelation has a profound impact on research data integrity and implications for data reproducibility across fields dependent on antibody specificity. This incident has put the spotlight on antibody suppliers to improve their processes to ensure properly validated products are being supplied to research labs.

item.title: Unveiling Neuronal Microstructure in the Human Brain In Vivo With Time‐Dependent Radial Diffusivity in a Head‐Only High‐Performance Gradient 3T MRI System
item.author: Ante Zhu, Jerome J. Maller, H. Douglas Morris, Jeffrey P. Guenette, Flavio Dell’ Acqua, Chu‐Yu Lee, Jeffrey McGovern, Stephan E. Maier, Raymond Y. Huang, Andrew L. Alexander, Maureen N. Hood, Desmond Teck Beng Yeo, Steven C. R. Williams, Carl‐Fredrik Westin, Vincent B. Ho, Vincent A. Magnotta, Hua Li
item.content:encoded: This preliminary study characterized time-dependent radial diffusivity in the human brain in vivo, finding consistently high values in the healthy corticospinal tract. These observations suggest that time-dependent radial diffusivity is sensitive to white matter microstructure associated with large axons, consistent with findings from preclinical studies.Diffusion time-dependence, defined as variations in diffusivity and/or diffusional kurtosis with diffusion time, has emerged as a valuable non-invasive imaging marker for characterizing tissue microstructural features, such as cell size, density, packing disorder, and membrane permeability. In white matter, diffusion time-dependent changes between the short diffusion time and long diffusion time in radial diffusivity (RD), defined as the diffusivity perpendicular to fiber tracts, were demonstrated to correlate strongly with mean axon diameter in ex vivo spinal cord tissues and to reveal demyelination in mouse corpus callosum. Oscillating gradient spin echo (OGSE) diffusion encoding can sample a high-frequency range of the diffusion spectral density, achieving a short effective diffusion time. Despite its potential to non-invasively unveil neuronal microstructures to improve the assessment and targeted therapy of neurological diseases, OGSE diffusion MRI has only recently become feasible for human in vivo studies with high-performance gradient MRI systems. In this preliminary study, we characterized time-dependent RD with OGSE encoding in the human brain in vivo. The change in radial diffusivity between short diffusion time and long diffusion time (ΔRD) consistently exhibited high values in the corticospinal tract, indicating high sensitivity of ΔRD to large axon diameter in human brains. Imaging at a high OGSE frequency of 100 Hz and a moderate -value of 800 × 10 ms/μm produced the highest ΔRD in the corticospinal tract. This study established a baseline for future investigations of neuronal microstructural alterations in neurological disorders and diseases.

item.title: Gene discovery and pleiotropic architecture of multidimensional pain in a genome-wide association study of >1.2 million individuals
item.author: Henry R. Kranzler
item.content:encoded: We conducted a meta-analytic genome-wide association study of multidimensional pain in >1.2 million European-ancestry individuals. We identified 343 independent loci, which, alongside findings from a sex-stratified GWAS and other analyses, expand our knowledge of the genetics of pain.

item.title: Synthetic torpor in the rat protects the heart from ischaemia-reperfusion injury
item.author: Una R Wilcox
item.content:encoded: During times of environmental stress, many animals enter torpor: a reversible protective physiological state typically characterised by reductions in core temperature, heart rate, and oxygen consumption. Species that naturally enter this hypothermic and hypometabolic state are tolerant of ischaemia-reperfusion injury. Consequently, there is a growing interest in utilising aspects of torpor for clinical applications such as protection from stroke or myocardial infarction. It is currently unknown, however, whether a torpor-like state is protective in animals that do not naturally enter torpor. Using viral vector-mediated chemogenetic activation of the medial preoptic area of the hypothalamus, we induced synthetic torpor in the rat, a species that does not naturally enter torpor. We demonstrate this state is cardioprotective in an ex vivo ischaemia-reperfusion injury model with an ~40% reduction in infarct size. Synthetic torpor-induced cardioprotection of the normothermic, isolated heart is not dependent on prior hypothermia in vivo. Phosphoproteomic analysis of cardiac tissue indicates that the protective effects of synthetic torpor may be mediated by parallel activation of cell survival and stress tolerance pathways and inhibition of cell death pathways. These findings provide important insights into the mechanisms of organ protective effects of synthetic torpor states with implications for future clinical translation in humans.

item.title: Learning-associated flexibility of cortical taste coding is impaired in Shank3 knockout mice
item.author: Gina G Turrigiano
item.content:encoded: The ability to update the valence of sensory perception to influence behavior is crucial for survival. A common phenotype in autism spectrum disorders (ASDs) is defects in sensory processing, but whether these defects impair flexible sensory encoding is largely unexplored. In particular, how genetic risk factors such as deletion affect the adaptability of cortical taste processing and downstream behavior is unknown. To address this gap, we performed two-photon calcium imaging during a conditioned taste aversion (CTA) learning paradigm, an ethologically relevant form of associative learning that depends on taste processing in the gustatory cortex (GC), to examine how knockout alters taste-related neuronal activity in GC and influences CTA learning. We found that GC neurons in knockout mice exhibited reduced stimulus-evoked suppression and increased trial-to-trial correlated variability during the acquisition of CTA memory. These activity changes, which likely reduced signal-to-noise ratio in GC, were associated with slower CTA acquisition in knockout mice. In both genotypes, CTA learning enhanced, while subsequent extinction reduced, taste discriminability in GC, and both extinction and the associated reduction in discriminability were faster in knockout than in wild-type mice. Together, these results show that loss is associated with destabilized cortical activity dynamics in GC, which may contribute to inefficient encoding and maintenance of learned taste aversion. These findings show that loss of compromises the ability of animals to update behavior to incorporate negative outcomes, and suggest this loss of flexibility may be an important feature of monogenic ASDs.

item.title: Brain Stiffness Correlation Networks in Healthy Older Adults Using Magnetic Resonance Elastography
item.author: KowsalyaDevi Pavuluri, John Huston III, Richard L. Ehman, Armando Manduca, Clifford R. Jack Jr, Matthew L. Senjem, David T. Jones, Yi Sui, Matthew C. Murphy
item.content:encoded: Using in vivo Magnetic Resonance Elastography, we mapped brain stiffness across 112 gray matter regions in 98 cognitively unimpaired older adults, then built stiffness correlation networks from those regional measurements. The networks show small-world topology ( = 2.44 at 5% density), revealing a systematic biomechanical architecture of the brain.Magnetic resonance elastography (MRE) quantifies tissue stiffness, a measure of microstructural integrity. While gray matter structural correlation networks are well established, the large-scale topological organization of stiffness correlation networks is not fully characterized. This study introduces the biomechanical covariance network framework, in which stiffness correlation networks reflect inter-individual covariation in regional stiffness across participants after adjusting for age, sex, regional gray matter volume, total intracranial volume, and scanner. We tested whether these networks exhibit small-world topology and how they differ from volume correlation networks. MRE-derived stiffness and MRI-derived gray matter volume maps were analyzed from 98 cognitively unimpaired older adults, and correlation networks of 112 gray matter regions were constructed using the Mayo Clinic Adult Lifespan Template (MCALT) ADIR-122 parcellation. The normalized clustering coefficient (γ$$ \gamma $$), normalized path length, and small-world index (σ$$ \sigma $$) were calculated against degree-preserving null networks across network densities. The stiffness correlation networks exhibited small-world architecture, with high local clustering and short path lengths (σ$$ \sigma $$ = 2.44 at 5% density and above 1 at all densities examined, 5%–51%). Stiffness and volume correlation networks showed partial correspondence ( = 0.306, < 0.0001) but were not redundant, with the stiffness networks showing stronger local clustering (γ$$ \gamma $$ = 3.01 versus 2.43 at 5% density). These findings establish the biomechanical covariance network framework in cognitively unimpaired older adults and suggest that biomechanical correlations may offer information complementary to volumetric measures. The framework provides a reference for future studies of how these networks change with age, disease, and cognitive decline.

item.title: Long-term training continually fine tunes motor memories
item.content:encoded: Humans’ rapid adaptation to new dynamics is a crucial ability for interacting with the world. By combining the controlled manipulations of sensorimotor adaptation studies with the long-term learning approach of complex tasks, this study shows that the learned motor memory is continually tuned, and that retention increases with long-term training.

item.author: Cicely F. Day, Alex A. Pollen, Madeline A. Lancaster
item.content:encoded: Day et al. review how neural organoids enable experimental investigation of human brain evolution. They examine insights across biological scales, from genetic changes to cellular diversity and timing, and discuss the opportunities and limitations of these models for connecting evolutionary changes in DNA to brain development and function.

item.title: Brain organoids: Experimental access to human-specific brain development
item.author: Rahel Kastli, Rebecca E. Andersen, Christopher A. Walsh, Paola Arlotta
item.content:encoded: Human brain development is largely inaccessible to mechanistic investigation, and evolutionarily divergent programs cannot be fully modeled in other species. Here, Kastli et al. review brain organoids as powerful experimental systems to unravel the mechanisms of human neurodevelopment and its neurodivergences.

item.title: Toward functional oversight of neural organoid research: A report from the 2025 Asilomar Conference
item.author: Brie Linkenhoker
item.content:encoded: In November 2025, an international multistakeholder group convened at Asilomar, California, to address oversight of rapidly advancing neural organoid and assembloid research. This process report documents the convening’s design, outcomes, and lessons, and it asks what it will take to turn this momentum into ongoing monitoring and practical guidelines that ensure responsible research without constraining scientific progress.

item.title: Cognitive evaluation of brain organoids and assembloids
item.author: Lucia Melloni, Stanislas Dehaene
item.content:encoded: The computational abilities of brain organoids and assembloids remain largely unexplored. We propose a hierarchy of assays grounded in cognitive neuroscience and probing representations, memory, and predictive processing, thus enabling causal tests of how architecture and maturation shape emerging computations while providing empirical constraints on debates about organoid consciousness.

item.title: Unbundling the ethical and social issues in human neural organoid research
item.author: Henry T. Greely, Nita Farahany
item.content:encoded: As human neural organoid research advances, some key concepts in its ethical analysis need to be unbundled to keep pace with scientific developments. These include interests involved in informed consent, distinct dimensions of consciousness and their implications for welfare, approaches to engaging public concerns, and governance and oversight of both organoids themselves and their uses.

item.title: Human stem cell neuroscience
item.author: Sergiu P. Pașca
item.content:encoded: In neuroscience, the most relevant human biology has often been the least accessible. Stem-cell-based models, such as organoids and assembloids, are opening ways to generate, assemble, probe, and perturb neural cells and circuits, helping define “stem cell neuroscience.” In this issue of Neuron, this and other reviews and commentaries discuss the current state of this emerging field.

item.title: Study planning is better served by Monte Carlo simulation than AI-generated participants
item.author: Jamie Cummins
item.content:encoded: ‘Silicon samples’, AI-generated synthetic data based on demographic profiles, have been proposed to help plan research. Here, I argue that Monte Carlo simulation already does this job transparently, and that generative AI is better used to help write such simulations.

item.title: Unequal causes and consequences of AI use
item.author: Yinghui Liang
item.content:encoded: Generative AI enters organizations rife with inequality. Here, we propose a recursive process whereby inequality can drive marginalized group members to use AI, but actual or suspected AI use can reinforce inequality through unequal judgement of communicators’ capability, credibility, and authenticity.

item.title: Cholinergic blockade reveals a role for human hippocampal theta in memory encoding but not retrieval
item.author: Tamara Gedankien
item.content:encoded: Cholinergic dysfunction is a hallmark of Alzheimer’s disease and other memory disorders. Yet, the neurophysiological mechanisms linking cholinergic signaling to memory remain poorly understood. In this study, we administered scopolamine, a muscarinic cholinergic antagonist, to neurosurgical patients with intracranial electrodes as they performed an associative recognition memory task. When scopolamine was present at encoding, we observed disruptions to hippocampal slow theta oscillations (2–4 Hz), with selective impairments to recollection-based memory. However, when scopolamine was present during retrieval alone, we observed disruptions to slow theta without impaired memory performance. These disruptions included dose-dependent reductions in theta power, theta phase reset, and encoding–retrieval pattern reinstatement. Together, our results challenge the notion that theta oscillations are necessary for memory retrieval, and instead suggest that theta universally reflects an encoding-related neural state. These findings motivate updates to current models of acetylcholine’s role in memory and may inform future therapies targeting rhythmic biomarkers of memory dysfunction.

item.title: Variability, but Not Concentration, of Neuromelanin in the Substantia Nigra Is Associated With Individual Differences in Interference Control
item.author: Shuhui Lyu, Hongchi Zhang, Jimin Yan, Jiaqi Gao, Kangcheng Wang, Lorenza Colzato, Bernhard Hommel
item.content:encoded: Differences in neuromelanin signal heterogeneity (NM-SD), not mean levels, predict interference control across sessions, suggesting a stable dopaminergic trait. However, this relationship weakens after accounting for voxel size, implying NM-SD reflects both biological variability and imaging-related factors.Interference control—the ability to suppress distracting information while selecting task-relevant responses—relies on dopaminergic modulation of fronto-striatal circuits. Although pharmacological evidence shows that transient dopaminergic enhancement can reduce interference, it remains unclear whether stable, trait-like properties of the dopaminergic system constrain individual differences in control efficiency. The present study examined whether the concentration of the neuromelanin signal (NM-Mean), and/or its variability, indexed by the standard deviation of the neuromelanin-sensitive MRI contrast-to-noise ratio (NM-SD), within the substantia nigra is associated with performance in the Flanker conflict task. Sixty healthy young adults completed the task. Neuromelanin CNR maps were registered to MNI152 standard space for ROI definition, and voxel-wise CNR values within the SN–VTA region were extracted in native space to derive NM-Mean and NM-SD. NM-Mean, indexing overall neuromelanin concentration, was not related to behavioral performance. In contrast, lower NM-SD, reflecting more homogeneous dopaminergic integrity, was associated with smaller Flanker interference effects but was unrelated to conflict adaptation across trials. Statistically controlling for voxel size rendered the effect size no longer significant, but a trend remained. These findings provide limited and preliminary evidence that individual differences in dopaminergic signal reliability, rather than overall dopamine quantity, contribute to variability in cognitive control. Although NM-SD is sensitive to acquisition-related factors such as spatial resolution, the observed attenuation of its association with interference control after controlling for voxel size suggests that its behavioral relevance may reflect a mixture of biological variability and methodological influences rather than a clear trait-like property of the dopaminergic system.

item.title: Network approaches to community detection in nanoscale connectomics
item.author: Richard Betzel
item.content:encoded: Extracting insight from nanoscale connectomes presents formidable challenges. In this Review, Betzel and colleagues focus on network science applications to these high-dimensional datasets, providing a high-level overview of different community detection methods while discussing which methods suit which questions and the types of biologically meaningful information they can reveal.

item.title: The cortico-basal ganglia–thalamic network: a connectomic framework
item.author: Houri Hintiryan
item.content:encoded: The cortico-basal ganglia–thalamic (CBGT) system supports a wide range of behaviours through its modular network organization. Dong and colleagues describe how advanced mesoscale and single-neuron connectomics has refined our understanding of CBGT circuit architecture, providing insights into the network’s capacity to preserve functional specialization while integrating across sensory, motor and cognitive domains.

item.title: Functional brain signatures of successful cognitive aging
item.author: Niklas Behrenbruch, Larissa Fischer, Hans Kirschner, Theresa M. Harrison, Anne Maass
item.content:encoded: Cognitive aging trajectories vary markedly. While many older adults experience gradual decline in memory and executive function, some maintain high cognitive performance well into advanced age. Understanding the neural mechanisms underlying this variability carries important implications for early detection of unfavorable aging trajectories and the development of interventions. Here, we review functional brain signatures associated with successful cognitive aging in humans, integrating evidence from functional magnetic resonance imaging and electroencephalography within a unified conceptual framework of brain maintenance and compensation. Across both modalities, evidence increasingly links successful cognitive aging to the preservation of youth-like neural dynamics, while the contribution of compensatory neural recruitment remains empirically contested and methodologically difficult to establish.

item.title: Information formatting in neuronal populations predicts differential functional contributions to behavior
item.author: Marlene R. Cohen
item.content:encoded: Using experiments in monkeys and modeling, the authors demonstrate that the formatting of population information predicts the contribution of different brain areas to behavior.

item.title: Midbrain somatostatin-expressing cells control pain-suppression during defensive states
item.author: Zoe Grivet
item.content:encoded: In threatening situations, animals exhibit a broad range of behavioral and autonomic responses. As such, a crucial adaptive response is the inhibition of pain, which facilitates relevant defensive behaviors that promote survival. Whereas the structures and mechanisms involved in fear and pain behaviors are well documented, little is known about the precise neuronal mechanisms mediating the emotional regulation of endogenous pain-suppression. Here, we used a combination of behavioral, anatomical, optogenetic, and electrophysiological approaches to investigate, in male mice, the role of somatostatin-expressing cells in the ventrolateral periaqueductal gray matter (SST vlPAG cells) in the control of analgesia induced during defensive states. Our data indicate that optogenetic inhibition of SST vlPAG cells promotes analgesia irrespective of animal defensive state. In contrast, optogenetic activation of long-range SST vlPAG cells that project to the rostral ventromedial medulla (RVM) abolishes the analgesia mediated by fear behavior. Together, these results identify a novel circuit mechanism composed of long-range SST vlPAG cells projecting to the RVM that regulate analgesia elicited during defensive states.

item.content:encoded: Schematic overview of the study design and main findings. This cross-sectional single-center study demonstrates that enlarged PVS volume in the basal ganglia (BG) subfields, particularly the caudate and putamen, is associated with worse cognitive function in CSVD. PVS burden increases with age and is more prominent in males, while hippocampal PVS enlargement inversely correlates with hippocampal volume and visuospatial function. These findings highlight regional PVS enlargement as a potential biomarker reflecting age and sex-related glymphatic dysfunction in CSVD.Perivascular spaces (PVS) serve as essential elements of the glymphatic pathway, facilitating waste clearance and nutrient transport, and their impairment may underlie cognitive deficits in cerebral small vessel disease (CSVD). Here, we investigated associations between PVS characteristics, potential determinants, and cognitive impairment in CSVD. 132 individuals diagnosed with CSVD and 40 healthy controls (HCs) were recruited to participate in a series of thorough neuropsychological assessments and neuroimaging examinations. PVS volume fraction (VF) was quantified in basal ganglia (BG), thalamus, hippocampus, and white matter (WM) using an automated, multimodal image processing pipeline (Enhanced PVS Contrast, EPC) combined with the Frangi filter for robust segmentation. Partial correlation analyses, adjusted for covariates, were performed. CSVD patients exhibited significantly larger PVS VF in the BG and hippocampus, particularly in caudate and putamen subfields of BG (all < 0.05). In CSVD group, advancing age correlated with elevated PVS VF in both BG and hippocampus, especially in males (all < 0.05). A main effect of sex on PVS VF was observed in this patient cohort across the BG, caudate, hippocampus and thalamus, where males exhibited larger PVS VF than females (all < 0.05). In HC group, age correlated positively with PVS volume fraction in the BG ( < 0.05), with no significant sex differences across regions. Enlarged BG-PVS was associated with worse global cognitive function (pr = −0.27, = 0.027) and processing speed (pr = −0.31, = 0.010), persisting after controlling for other neuroimaging markers (including WMHs, lacunes, and CMBs) and regional volume. Subfield analyses revealed the correlation mainly occurring in the putamen (pr = −0.31, = 0.010). Hippocampal PVS VF inversely correlated with hippocampal volume (pr = −0.26, = 0.043), more pronounced in females, and was significantly linked to worse visuospatial function (pr = −0.33, = 0.010). Regional PVS enlargement in CSVD, particularly in BG and hippocampus regions, reflects underlying glymphatic impairment related to age and sex. The prominence of this finding within BG subregions further underscores their role in the pathogenesis of neurocognitive decline.

item.title: Dual-feature selectivity enables bidirectional coding in visual cortical neurons
item.author: Tori Shinn
item.content:encoded: Sensory neurons are traditionally viewed as feature detectors that respond with an increase in firing rate to preferred stimuli while remaining unresponsive to others. Here, we identify a dual-feature encoding strategy in macaque visual cortex, wherein many neurons in areas V1 and V4 are selectively tuned to two distinct visual features—one that enhances and one that suppresses activity—around an elevated baseline firing rate. By combining neuronal recordings with functional digital twin models—deep learning-based predictive models of biological neurons—we were able to systematically identify each neuron’s preferred and non-preferred features. These feature pairs served as anchors for a continuous, low-dimensional axis in natural image similarity space, along which neuronal activity varied approximately linearly. Within a single visual area, visual features that strongly or weakly activated individual neurons also had a high probability of modulating the activity of other neurons, suggesting a shared feature selectivity across the population that structures stimulus encoding. We show that this encoding strategy is conserved across species, present in both primary and lateral visual areas of mouse cortex. Dual-feature selectivity is consistent with recent anatomical evidence for feature-specific inhibitory connectivity, complementing the feature-detector principle through circuit mechanisms in which selective excitation and inhibition may together enhance the representational capacity of the neuronal population.

item.title: Intrasubject Reconfiguration of the Cortical Gradients' Topological Properties With Cognitive States
item.author: Derek J. Pavelka, Attakias T. Mertens, Katrina Myers, Callum Goldsmith, Joanna Arch, Jessica R. Andrews‐Hanna, Gaelle E. Doucet
item.content:encoded: Cortical gradients' topological properties were computed in 138 healthy young individuals across four fMRI tasks. Our findings suggest the gradients' topological properties are sensitive to different cognitive and attentional demands.Cortical gradients have been shown to be an effective technique to study the functional organization of the brain by capturing patterns of functional similarities. Until now, most studies have focused on analyzing cortical gradients derived from resting-state fMRI. With recent work highlighting the changes that functional brain networks undergo during various cognitive loads, there is a need to investigate whether cortical gradients are also sensitive to different cognitive demands, and to what degree. In this context, we collected a sample of 138 healthy individuals aged 12–25, each of whom completed a resting-state fMRI scan as well as three task fMRI scans (social prospection, spatial working memory, and verbal working memory). All data were analyzed to examine the task dependence of cortical gradients' topological properties. By employing the measures of network gradient dispersions as well as networks centroid distances, we revealed that alterations specific to each task occurred in topological properties of gradients involving both transmodal and unimodal networks, such as the executive control network varying between each task condition and the resting-state condition. This work highlights the promise of applying cortical gradients to task-based fMRI data, revealing the condition-sensitive nature of certain cortical gradients' topological properties.

item.title: Exposure to Maternal Pre‐ and Postnatal Psychological Distress: Associations With Brain Structure in 5‐Year‐Old Children
item.author: Elmo P. Pulli, Hilyatushalihah K. Audah, Amira Svensk, Eeva Eskola, Elisabeth Nordenswan, Aylin Rosberg, Silja Alvajärvi, Pauliina Juntunen, Isabella L. C. item.content:encoded: This study provides support for hypotheses proposing that early-life exposure to maternal distress can influence the structural development of the brain. Furthermore, it highlights the role of the early postnatal period and calls for further research into this so far overlooked period and pathways that explain the associations.Maternal mental health is an important contributor to child neurodevelopment. While there are multiple studies on prenatal exposure, early postnatal exposure has received little attention in neuroimaging research. Five-year-old children ( = 161) were recruited from the FinnBrain Birth Cohort study. Maternal distress was assessed using questionnaires on depressive and anxiety symptoms at 14, 24, and 34 gestational weeks and postnatally at 3, 6, and 24 months. T1-weighted structural images were processed using a voxel-based morphometry pipeline to map associations between maternal distress exposure and regional gray matter (GM) volumes. Whole-brain voxel-wise general linear models were used, accounting for potential confounders. Additionally, a latent class mixed model approach was used to model longitudinal trajectories of distress exposure. We found widespread associations between maternal postpartum distress symptoms and offspring brain morphology. Postnatal distress at 3 months was negatively associated with GM volumes in the left supplementary motor cortex, right cerebellum/fusiform gyrus, and left anterior insula/frontal operculum. Postnatal distress at 6 months was positively associated with GM volumes in the right cuneus and lingual gyrus, right insula/operculum, and right inferior occipital gyrus, while distress at 24 months was negatively associated with GM volumes in the left inferior/middle frontal gyrus. There were no structural brain differences between the latent classes. This study provides support for hypotheses proposing that early-life exposure to maternal distress can influence the structural development of the brain. It highlights the role of the early postnatal period and calls for further research into this so far overlooked period and the developmental pathways that explain these associations.

item.title: Consumer neuroscience: the emerging science of everyday choices
item.author: Hilke Plassmann, Uma Karmarkar, Vinod Venkatraman
item.content:encoded: Consumer neuroscience is a developing field at the intersection of neuroscience, psychology, economics, and marketing that seeks to uncover the neural and physiological mechanisms underlying consumer behavior. Building on early psychophysiological studies, the field has expanded substantially since the mid-2000s through an increasing range of methods and models. We highlight that its strength lies in spanning multiple levels of analysis to address marketing-relevant questions. We highlight four major trends driving the field: improving behavioral prediction, synthesizing evidence through multidataset analyses, developing formal models linking neural processes to consumer decision-making, and integrating brain and body measures. Together, these advances position consumer neuroscience as an integrative science with implications for marketing, policy, and consumer welfare.

item.title: Constructing events across perception, action, and thought
item.author: Dasom Kwon, Jiwoong Park, Won Mok Shim
item.content:encoded: The brain organizes continuous experience into events that structure episodic memory and guide behavior. Traditional accounts have primarily focused on sensory discontinuities and prediction errors that trigger updates of event models. Here, we broaden this view to consider event boundaries arising during goal-directed behavior, spontaneous thought, and memory recall, including transitions generated in the absence of corresponding changes in sensory input. We propose that prediction error and uncertainty provide complementary signals for event model updating: prediction errors signal a violation of current expectations, whereas uncertainty may promote updating when upcoming states become difficult to predict. We further suggest that the hippocampus may serve as a candidate hub linking boundary-related representational changes across perception, action, and thought. Together, this framework offers an integrative account of how the brain detects and generates event structure in continuous experience to support memory and behavior.

item.title: Simple methods to acutely measure multiple timing metrics among the sexual repertoire of male Drosophila
item.author: Yutong Song
item.content:encoded: Male courtship behavior is a key model for studying temporal decision-making. While courtship index (CI) is widely used to quantify mating activity, other timing metrics like courtship latency, copulation latency (CL), and mating duration (MD) remain understudied. Traditional methods for quantifying these behaviors are often labor-intensive and prone to human error. In this study, we present a protocol combining a modular chamber system and automated software (DrosoMating) to quantify six key timing metrics during male courtship. Our image-based video analysis enables precise identification of courtship and copulation events, as well as quantification of their timing and duration under controlled conditions. Validation shows <0.05% error rates and 98–99% agreement with manual scoring for CL, CI, and MD. The protocol supports genetic and neural circuit manipulations, detecting subtle genetic, social, and environmental behavioral variations. By minimizing manual effort and standardizing data collection, this approach facilitates scalable, reproducible studies on adaptive trade-offs, learning, and neural mechanisms in mating behavior. This method streamlines timing analysis in male courtship, offering reproducible metrics for behavioral genetics.

item.title: The hypoxic response extends lifespan through a bioaminergic and peptidergic neural circuit
item.author: Shijiao Huang
item.content:encoded: A coordinated response to stress is crucial for promoting the short- and long-term health of an organism. The perception of stress, frequently through the nervous system, can lead to physiological changes that are fundamental to maintaining homeostasis. Activating the response to low oxygen, or hypoxia, extends healthspan and lifespan in . However, despite some positive impacts, negative effects of the hypoxic response in specific tissues prevent translation of their benefits in mammals. Thus, it is imperative to identify which components of this response promote longevity. Here, we interrogate the cell-nonautonomous signaling pathway downstream of genetic activation of the hypoxic response. We find that HIF-1-mediated signaling in ADF serotonergic neurons is both necessary and sufficient for lifespan extension. Signaling through the serotonin receptor SER-7 in the GABAergic RIS interneurons is necessary in this process. Our findings also highlight the involvement of additional neural signaling molecules, including the neurotransmitters tyramine and GABA, and the neuropeptide NLP-17, in mediating longevity effects. Finally, we demonstrate that oxygen- and carbon-dioxide-sensing neurons act downstream of HIF-1 in this circuit. Together, these insights demonstrate a circuit for how genetic induction of the hypoxic response cell-nonautonomously modifies aging and suggests valuable targets for modulating aging in mammals.

item.title: The resource elasticity of control
item.author: Levi Solomyak
item.content:encoded: The ability to determine how much the environment can be controlled through our actions has long been viewed as fundamental to adaptive behavior. While traditional accounts treat controllability as a fixed property of the environment, we argue that real-world controllability often depends on the effort, time, and money we are able and willing to invest. In such cases, controllability can be said to be to invested resources. Here, we propose that inferring this elasticity is essential for efficient resource allocation, and thus, elasticity misestimations result in maladaptive behavior. To test this hypothesis, we developed a novel treasure hunt game where participants encountered environments with varying degrees of controllability and elasticity. Across two pre-registered studies (=514), we first demonstrate that people infer elasticity and adapt their resource allocation accordingly. We then present a computational model that explains how people make this inference and identify individual elasticity biases that lead to suboptimal resource allocation. Finally, we show that overestimation of elasticity is associated with elevated psychopathology involving an impaired sense of control. These findings establish the elasticity of control as a distinct cognitive construct guiding adaptive behavior and a computational marker for control-related maladaptive behavior.

item.title: Expectation-driven gain modulation of preparatory spatial attention
item.author: Stefan van der Stigchel
item.content:encoded: The visual system can flexibly adjust attentional deployment to match task demands, but whether observers can proactively modulate the spatial scope of attention based on expectations about upcoming search difficulty remains unclear. According to the zoom lens model, attention can narrow or broaden its spatial extent, with narrower focus enhancing processing efficiency, a mechanism that would benefit target discrimination in crowded displays. We tested whether observers adjust attentional scope when expecting sparse versus dense search arrays by combining spatial cueing with block-wise manipulations of display density expectations. Participants performed a visual search task in which endogenous cues predicted target location, while blocks predominantly contained either sparse (1 target, 3 distractors) or dense (1 target, 7 distractors) displays. We applied inverted encoding models to broadband EEG data to reconstruct spatial channel tuning functions, enabling precise characterization of both the locus and breadth of attentional deployment. Behaviorally, expecting difficult searches selectively improved accuracy at cued locations without costs elsewhere. Consistent with this selective benefit, neural measurements revealed that expectancy enhanced the amplitude of spatially selective responses at the attended location but did not alter tuning width. These findings demonstrate that expectations about search difficulty modulate attention through gain-based signal enhancement rather than adjustments to spatial scope, revealing that preparatory attentional control operates via amplitude modulation within a stable spatial focus. This mechanism complements reactive attentional adjustments and provides an efficient means for the visual system to optimize processing under predictable task demands.

item.title: Distinct neural representations of perceptual and numerical absence in the human brain
item.author: Stephen M Fleming
item.content:encoded: The ability to represent absences is fundamental to human perception and cognition. Sensitivity to non-numerical absences depends on inferring a lack of sensory evidence, enabling the recognition of a lack of environmental resources or other objects. In turn, encoding numerical absence as a concept – in the form of the number zero – has enabled a multitude of technological and mathematical advances. Whether perceptual and conceptual absences rely on overlapping or distinct neural representations in the human brain, however, remains unknown. We employed three different tasks together with magnetoencephalography to characterise neural representations of absence evoked within perceptual and numerical domains. Using multivariate decoding and Bayes factor analyses, we replicate previous findings of shared representations of numerical absence across symbolic and non-symbolic formats. In contrast, we show that these representations of numerical absence are distinct from those evoked by non-numerical absences. This result held even after controlling for stimulus-level confounds which generate surface-level similarities between perceptual absences and non-symbolic empty sets. Our results extend a boundary between perception and cognition to the domain of absence and provide insight into the different mechanisms employed by the human brain to both perceive and conceive of absences.

item.title: Spectraplakin is required for dendritic microtubule organization via a tip-based mechanism in Drosophila
item.author: Yitao Shen
item.content:encoded: The differential microtubule organization in axons and dendrites underlies neuronal polarity and developmental processes, like neurite pruning. How neurons achieve their specific microtubule organization during development is an area of active research, and it has been especially hard to explain how dendritic microtubules are oriented with their plus ends toward the soma. Transient microtubule nucleation from tips of early growing dendrites has been proposed as a mechanism that would explain how this orientation is set up. In a survey for cytoskeletal regulators involved in dendrite pruning and microtubule organization in , we found the spectraplakin Short stop (Shot), an actin/microtubule crosslinker. Loss of Shot causes microtubule orientation defects already during early dendrite development, when Shot is transiently recruited to tips of growing dendrites via its actin-binding domain. Genetic and functional evidence suggests that Shot’s primary function in this process is to locally stabilize microtubules. We also provide evidence for an independent, developmentally transient microtubule nucleation mechanism. Our data highlight the importance of transient and localized microtubule regulation for dendritic microtubule organization.

item.title: Dopaminergic neurons linking threat processing to cardiac modulation and locomotor responses
item.author: Yuki Uemura
item.content:encoded: Heartbeat and behavior are tightly coordinated during defensive states, yet the neuronal mechanisms linking threat processing to cardiac modulation—and the potential contribution of cardiac dynamics to behavioral output—remain poorly understood. Here, using simultaneous recordings of heartbeat and behavior in tethered , we show that mechanical threat triggers locomotion together with rapid cardiac deceleration. We identify two pairs of dopaminergic neurons, termed DA-WED neurons, that mediate this cardiac response. Silencing these neurons markedly attenuates threat-induced cardiac deceleration, whereas optogenetic activation induces cardiac deceleration in the absence of threat. Two-photon calcium imaging further shows that DA-WED neurons are activated by mechanical threat, and manipulating their activity bidirectionally modulates threat-induced locomotion. Linking cardiac dynamics to behavior, direct optogenetic manipulation of cardiomyocytes that quantitatively reproduces threat-evoked cardiac deceleration is accompanied by increased locomotion. Together, these results identify a dopaminergic descending pathway that links threat processing to cardiac modulation and suggest that cardiac dynamics may contribute to shaping defensive behavior.

item.title: Lost, then found: transient forgetting in humans and machines
item.author: Milan Van Maldegem, Hans Op de Beeck, Niels A. Taatgen, Tinne Tuytelaars, Gido M. van de Ven
item.content:encoded: Forgetting can be permanent or transient. An intriguing, recently described form of transient forgetting (TF) in artificial neural networks is the stability gap: a network that has already learned a first task exhibits transient yet substantial forgetting when it begins additional training on a second task alongside the first. Could an analogous phenomenon be found in humans? Following a literature survey, six types of TF in humans were identified, categorised by their sources: learning, retrieval, spontaneous, overgeneralisation, task-switching, and multitasking. Although all differ in important ways from the stability gap, it is hypothesised that some underlying mechanisms are shared. This opinion article concludes by proposing experiments to test whether a ‘stability gap-like’ form of TF also occurs in humans.

item.title: What can behavior tell us about neural dynamics?
item.author: Fanny Cazettes, Marieke L. Schölvinck
item.content:encoded: For decades, systems neuroscience treated behavior as an endpoint: a simplified output, such as a button press, lick, or saccade, used to isolate neural computations. Richer behavioral measurements have expanded this view by revealing neural dynamics hidden by simple outputs. Yet behavior is not a direct readout of brain activity, because similar behavioral outputs can arise from different neural mechanisms. Interpreting neural dynamics is therefore an inverse problem with no straightforward solution. Behavior can constrain this problem by exposing sensorimotor loops, narrowing plausible explanations for population activity, and formalizing neural–behavioral relationships in joint models. Together, these approaches position behavior as a principled constraint on interpreting neural dynamics and latent cognitive, affective, and computational states.

item.title: Evolving perspectives on cardiac innervation: from relay to a complex regulated network
item.author: Beth A. Habecker, Johanna M. Montgomery
item.content:encoded: Neural control of the heart adjusts cardiac output to the functional demands of the body in order to maintain homeostasis. Sensory afferents monitor blood pressure, metabolites, and other parameters, sending information to the brainstem that then alters the balance of stimulatory sympathetic and inhibitory parasympathetic transmission to the heart. ‘Autonomic imbalance’ between sympathetic and parasympathetic efferent transmission in the heart is a characteristic of cardiovascular and metabolic diseases that contributes to pathology. In this review, we discuss recent studies related to the peripheral components of the cardiac control circuit. We summarize data from induced pluripotent stem cells, small and large animal models, and human studies that reveal more complexity in peripheral components of this system than previously understood. We also discuss peripheral neuroplasticity in cardiovascular disease and the potential impact of neuromodulation therapies.

item.title: A validated antibody toolbox for ALS research
item.author: Zhipeng You
item.content:encoded: A substantial fraction of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)-associated proteins remains poorly characterized, in part because of the limited availability of validated research antibodies. We established knockout (KO)-based antibody characterization workflows and demonstrated that widely used antibodies against the major ALS-associated protein C9orf72 lacked specificity (Laflamme et al., 2019). We subsequently scaled this framework to systematically benchmark research antibodies, revealing that up to 61% fail to perform as recommended by manufacturers (Ayoubi et al., 2023b). Here, we extend this approach by establishing the ALS-Reproducible Antibody Platform (ALS-RAP), a comprehensive effort to generate a publicly available dataset of KO-validated antibodies targeting proteins encoded by ALS risk genes. In total, we characterized 303 antibodies against 33 ALS-associated proteins to identify high-quality reagents for use in western blot, immunoprecipitation, and immunofluorescence. Using these antibodies, we profiled protein levels across human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived and primary neurological cell types. These analyses revealed diverse cellular distributions and higher levels of several ALS-associated proteins in glial populations, consistent with emerging evidence for immune contributions to ALS. Together, ALS-RAP provides a validated antibody toolbox and protein expression resource to support the study of ALS-associated proteins.

item.title: SPARK‐ICA: Guided Frequency‐Resolved Dynamic Spatial ICA Reveals Fine‐Scale fMRI Network Dynamics
item.author: N. Behzadfar, A. Iraji, V. Calhoun
item.content:encoded: SPARK–ICA is a frequency-resolved dynamic spatial ICA framework that decomposes time-varying fMRI network maps into multiple spatial frequency bands. Applied to schizophrenia resting-state data, it reveals complementary abnormalities in stable connectivity and rapid high-frequency network interactions that are not captured by conventional dynamic connectivity analyses.Fine-scale spatiotemporal dynamics of functional brain networks are increasingly recognized as critical markers of transient connectivity and neuropsychiatric pathology. However, many existing dynamic fMRI methods primarily focus on temporal variability without explicitly resolving the spatial-frequency content of network dynamics, potentially limiting characterization of subtle, high-frequency spatial reconfigurations. To address this gap, we propose SPARK–ICA (Spatial–frequency Partitioned, Adaptive Reconstruction using Knowledge-guided ICA), a frequency-resolved dynamic spatial independent component analysis (ICA) framework that integrates NeuroMark template guidance with spatial frequency decomposition and group-level ICA of time-resolved, band-specific spatial maps. Starting from template-guided NeuroMark networks, we first estimate time-varying spatial maps using a dynamic guided ICA approach, capturing subject-specific network expression over time. Each dynamic spatial map is then decomposed into multiple spatial frequency bands using Fourier-domain spatial filtering, isolating fine- to coarse-scale spatial features at each time point. Band-specific spatial maps are subsequently concatenated and subjected to a blind group-level multi-frequency ICA, yielding a compact latent representation in which each dynamic component is characterized by distinct spatial-frequency signatures. These group-level band-resolved components are then used as references to estimate subject- and band-specific time courses and maps via spatially constrained ICA, enabling frequency-specific analysis of both long-term correlations and short-term temporal variability while preserving reproducibility across subjects. Using resting-state fMRI data from schizophrenia (SZ) patients and healthy controls (HC), we evaluated both long-term correlations and short-term variability of band-resolved dynamic time courses. For the group-level analyses, we focused on a predefined subset of NeuroMark networks with well-established involvement in SZ-related dysconnectivity. Our results reveal frequency-specific abnormalities in SZ, with enhanced long-term connectivity within sensory and subcortical networks and pronounced short-term alterations involving predominantly higher-frequency spatial components, particularly in cerebellar and subcortical systems. These findings indicate that SZ-related dysregulation is differentially expressed across spatial-frequency and temporal scales, rather than reflecting uniform dysconnectivity. Together, this framework provides a unified approach for analyzing dynamic fMRI networks across spatial, temporal, and frequency dimensions, extending our previous NeuroMark-DyFICA framework from a predominantly high-frequency spatial representation to an explicitly frequency-resolved characterization of dynamic network organization. By explicitly modeling spatial frequency–dependent dynamics, the proposed method provides a more resolved characterization of network alterations and offers a framework for identifying candidate markers of neuropsychiatric disorders.

item.title: Behavioural and neurogenetic evidence for emotion primitives in the fruit fly Drosophila from an open field test
item.author: Yi Lueningschroer-Wang
item.content:encoded: Emotions are based on evolutionarily conserved building blocks (‘emotion primitives’) that are present across mammals. Whether these building blocks are found in insects is largely undefined. Here, we employ the open field test (OFT) in and focus on wall-following and total walking activity as behavioural indicators of emotion-like states. Wildtype and transgenic flies were subjected to various conditions prior to behavioural testing. The results indicate that wall-following and total walking activity are independent measures that are modulated, with generally increased wall-following observed under aversive stimuli and decreased values under positive conditions, independent of the time of day. The effects of genetic manipulation of selected neuromodulatory systems support their role in modulating emotion-like states in . Activation of reward-related neurons decreased wall-following while inhibition increased it. Moreover, treatment with ethanol or diazepam produced predictable changes in behaviour. Our findings suggest that shares conserved core emotion-like building blocks with vertebrates, and show that wall-following and total walking activity in the OFT can serve as a reliable indicator of emotional valence and arousal in the fruit fly. This positions as a powerful genetic model to dissect the neuronal and neurochemical substrates of emotion primitives.

item.title: THE MOST INFLUENTIAL ARTIST NOBODY KNOWS #history #arthistory #painting #artist #art
item.author: Great Art Explained
item.content:encoded:
Pierre Puvis de Chavannes (1824–1898) was one of the most influential French painters of the nineteenth century, although today he is far less well known than many of the artists he inspired. At a time when Impressionism was transforming painting with its fascination for modern life, light and movement, Puvis looked in an entirely different direction. His paintings depict quiet, dreamlike worlds populated by mysterious figures in timeless landscapes, where very little seems to happen, yet everything feels strangely significant.
Best known for his monumental murals in public buildings, Puvis developed a distinctive style characterised by muted colours, simplified forms, flattened perspectives and an almost complete absence of drama. His figures often appear detached from reality, suspended somewhere between classical antiquity and the modern world.
Although his work might appear conservative today, it was remarkably innovative. By rejecting naturalism in favour of atmosphere, symbolism and emotional suggestion, Puvis helped open the door to modern art. His influence can be traced through Gauguin, Seurat, Matisse and even the young Picasso. He was admired by artists who would go on to challenge almost everything nineteenth-century painting stood for, making him one of the most important, and perhaps most overlooked, bridges between academic tradition and modernism.

item.title: Functional Network Organization Underlying Individual Differences in False Feedback Susceptibility: A Graph Theoretical Analysis
item.author: J. Patchitt, T. Karapanagiotidis, S. N. Garfinkel, M. Miller, M. Tsakiris, A. Clark, H. D. Critchley
item.content:encoded: Individual differences in susceptibility to somatosensory false feedback (sFFB) predict altered network topography between regions previously implicated in sFFB. This work supports an interoceptive integration model of sFFB and highlights the importance of network topology in determining how individuals weigh and integrate internal and external physiological information during emotional processing.Individual differences in susceptibility to somatosensory false physiological feedback reflect variations in interoceptive processing, yet the underlying neural network mechanisms remain unclear. We analyzed resting-state functional connectivity using graph theoretical approaches in 41 healthy adults who completed a somatosensory false feedback paradigm. Nine regions of interest were defined from previous activation analyses, and network topology metrics including local efficiency, clustering coefficient, centrality measures, and path length were calculated across multiple thresholds. Three distinct patterns of network organization predicted false feedback susceptibility. Individuals more susceptible to false feedback showed: (1) increased posterior insula eccentricity, indicating network peripheralization of this key interoceptive region; (2) consistent orbitofrontal cortex segregation across multiple metrics including increased path length and decreased centrality measures; and (3) cerebellar network reconfiguration with reduced local efficiency but increased betweenness centrality. Somatosensory false feedback susceptibility reflects specific alterations in functional network topology, particularly reduced integration of interoceptive regions (posterior insula) and emotional appraisal systems (orbitofrontal cortex). These findings support a network-based model where interoceptive processing depends on efficient integration between visceral sensation, emotional evaluation, and cognitive control systems. Understanding these network properties may inform interventions targeting interoceptive awareness and emotional regulation.

item.title: Compensation of hyperexcitability with simulation-based inference
item.author: Tomoki Fukai
item.content:encoded: The activity of healthy neuronal networks is tightly regulated, and a shift toward hyperexcitability can cause various problems, such as epilepsies, memory deficits, and motor disorders. Numerous cellular, synaptic, and intrinsic mechanisms of hyperexcitability and compensatory mechanisms to restore healthy activity have been proposed. However, quantifying multiple compensatory mechanisms and their dependence on specific pathophysiological mechanisms has proven challenging, even in computational models. We use simulation-based inference to quantify the interactions of putative compensatory mechanisms in a spiking neuronal network model. Various parameters of the model can compensate for the changes in other parameters to maintain baseline activity, and we estimated their compensatory potential. Furthermore, specific causes of hyperexcitability – interneuron loss, excitatory recurrent synapses, and principal cell depolarization – have distinct compensatory mechanisms that can restore normal excitability. Our results show that spiking neuronal network simulators could generate hypotheses about the mechanisms of pathophysiological network mechanisms.

item.title: Fitness level, but not sex, affects exercise-induced pain modulation
item.author: Zora Pia Gerbers
item.content:encoded: In a previous study by our group (Nold et al., 2025), we investigated exercise-induced pain modulation after high-intensity compared to low-intensity exercise in a heterogeneous sample of diverse fitness levels. Exploratory analyses suggested an interaction of sex, fitness level, and drug treatment, indicating that males showed increasing hypoalgesia after high- compared to low-intensity exercise with increasing fitness levels, which was diminished when naloxone was administered. In contrast, these effects were not evident in females. These exploratory findings warranted further investigation to determine if and to what extent exercise-induced pain modulation depends on fitness level and/or sex. In this current study, we investigated an all-female sample (N=21) of high fitness levels using a similar paradigm as in the previous study, comparing heat and pressure pain ratings after high-intensity and low-intensity exercise. Our data show an interaction of exercise intensity and stimulus intensity in heat pain, with greater pain relief following high-intensity exercise, especially at the highest stimulus intensity. Despite results for pressure pain not reaching significance, a similar trend was evident. These results suggest that females at a high fitness level also show exercise-induced pain modulation for high-intensity compared to low-intensity exercise. Furthermore, we pooled the data of the current and previous study, providing evidence for fitness level but not sex to moderate exercise-induced pain modulation in heat pain. These findings suggest that exercise-induced pain modulation depends on fitness level but not on sex.

item.title: Oxytocin neurons signal state-dependent transitions from rest to thermogenesis and behavioral arousal
item.author: Samantha Killmer
item.content:encoded: Core body temperature (Tb) is defended within narrow limits through thermoregulatory behaviors like huddling, nesting, and physical activity, as well as autonomic responses like brown fat thermogenesis. While Tb displays regulated fluctuations across different behavioral states and rest/arousal cycles, the neural control of these transitions remains poorly understood. Here, we investigate the relationship between oxytocin neurons of the paraventricular hypothalamus (PVN) and behavioral and autonomic thermoeffector pathways across physiological states in mice. First, we show that PVN neurons are activated during social thermoregulation. We then demonstrate that in vivo PVN calcium dynamics align with transitions from rest to thermogenesis and behavioral arousal. Counter to our initial hypothesis, these dynamics were observed in both social and non-social contexts. Using a computer vision model to track thermoeffector pathways, we demonstrate that precisely timed stimulation of PVN neurons during low-Tb resting states increases thermogenesis followed by behavioral arousal. We therefore suggest a model in which PVN neurons facilitate homeostatic state-dependent transitions in thermo-behavioral states.

item.title: Glutamate receptor composition at Drosophila neuromuscular junctions depends on developmental stage and muscle identity
item.author: Yu Xiong
item.content:encoded: The neuromuscular junction (NMJ) of larval is widely used for studying synaptic transmission. Larval body wall muscles express five ionotropic glutamate receptor (iGluR) subunits that assemble into two tetrameric complexes, with subunit composition determining the strength and plasticity of synaptic transmission. Because NMJ function has been extensively characterized in larvae, it has commonly been assumed that adult fly NMJs share this molecular composition, despite substantial differences between life stages. Here, we systematically compare glutamate receptor expression across larval and adult muscles. We find that adult leg and flight muscles exhibit different iGluR expression than larvae, lacking expression of several receptors previously considered essential. Adjacent muscles within the adult femur express distinct iGluRs, suggesting specialization of flexor and extensor muscles. Finally, the glutamate-gated chloride channel (GluClα) is expressed extrasynaptically in adult but not larval muscle fibers. Our results reveal unexpected heterogeneity in glutamate receptor expression across muscles and developmental stages, demonstrating the need for muscle-specific analyses in flies and other animals.

item.title: Distinct gradients of cortical architecture capture visual representations and behavior across the lifespan
item.author: Zonglei Zhen
item.content:encoded: The microstructure of cells within the human cerebral cortex varies across the cortical ribbon, where changes in cytoarchitecture and myeloarchitecture are thought to endow each region of the cortex with its unique function. While fine-scale relative to a cell, these changes at the population level impact architectural properties of the cortex measurable in vivo by noninvasive MRI, such as the thickness and myelin content of the cortex. This raises the question of whether or not we can use these in vivo architectural measures to understand cortical organization, function, and development more broadly. Using the human visual cortex as a test bed, we demonstrated two architectural gradients, one in which cytoarchitecture and myeloarchitecture converge and another in which they diverge. These two gradients underlie the structural and functional topography of the visual cortex, even predicting the presence of new visual representations. Moreover, the two gradients show distinct visual behavior relevance and lifespan trajectory. These findings provide a more general framework for understanding the human cortex, showing that architectural gradients are a measurable fingerprint of functional organization and ontogenetic routines in the human brain.

item.title: Peripersonal space: a neural system mapping self–environment interaction ‘here and now’
item.author: Andrea Serino
item.content:encoded: The space surrounding the body where physical interactions with external stimuli occur is referred to as peripersonal space (PPS). Traditionally conceived as a spatial construct, PPS is better understood as a neural representation that integrates bodily inputs with external cues to predict body–object interactions. After summarizing its multisensory, motor, and plastic properties, this review draws on computational models to examine how PPS captures statistical regularities of body–object interactions. This predictive function may position PPS as an interface between self and environment, contributing to minimal self-consciousness and its alterations across states of consciousness and neuropsychiatric conditions. Recent findings extend this framework to the inner body, suggesting that interoceptive signals shape PPS and that PPS-related processing may influence immune responses.

item.title: Strength-based organizational approaches facilitate workplace opportunities for people from lower socioeconomic status backgrounds.
item.content:encoded: The workplace stands as one of the most powerful drivers of societal (in)equality. For employees from lower socioeconomic status backgrounds, it can represent both a ticket toward upward mobility and a consequential source of stigma. Four studies build on emerging strength-based research to test whether workplaces can challenge this stigma by creating overarching cultures that recognize the beneficial skills employees gain from their otherwise marginalized identities. Study 1 provided foundational insights into these “strength-based organizational approaches” and their implications for key outcomes derived from the State Authenticity as Fit to Environment model. Employees from lower socioeconomic status backgrounds were especially unlikely to report that their workplaces valued their identities and associated skills, which partially explained subsequent disparities in employees’ broad sense of comfort and efficacy at work. Studies 2a and 2b established these patterns experimentally by demonstrating that exposing participants to a workplace that does communicate a strength-based organizational approach facilitated these professionally productive outcomes while increasing participants’ likelihood of disclosing their marginalized identities within a job application task. Study 3 extended these findings to consider how the approaches may also indirectly expand employees’ equitable access to opportunity through reducing common biases among their supervisors. Randomly assigning workplace supervisors to briefly engage with a company that highlighted the value of employees’ lower socioeconomic status backgrounds increased supervisors’ positive evaluations and likelihood of promoting these employees by 38% relative to an active control condition. Collectively, these preregistered findings illuminate new opportunities to improve workplace functioning and pinpoint the organizational forces underlying person–context interactions. item.title: How we see relations: The case of containment and support.
item.content:encoded: To navigate and act in the environment, it is necessary to recognize objects and the relationships between them. Recognition of objects in visual scenes is rapid and automatic. Are relations between objects in a scene also extracted rapidly and automatically during perception? Here, we considered containment and support, two relations that are fundamental to our understanding of the physical world. Using frequency-tagging electroencephalography on human subjects, we measured stimulus-driven neural responses during rapid visual presentation of images (4 Hz), with a periodic oddball structure to isolate the selective response to object pairs presented side-by-side (e.g., a book and a table) versus two objects in support or containment relations (e.g., a book on a table). We found enhanced responses to objects in support/containment relations (vs. objects side-by-side) when a relation was instantiated by different exemplars of the same scene (e.g., a book on a table), but not by different scenes involving distinct object categories (e.g., a book on a table, a lamp on a stand, a laptop on a desk). These findings indicate that, during scene perception, relations are extracted in a format that generalizes within, but not across, types of visual scenes. We propose that, during perception, relations are not represented as discrete, abstract tokens (“in” or “on”) but rather as objects’ properties, such that changes in the objects entail changes in the relational representation. These results provide new insight into the perceptual foundations of relational processing underlying physical reasoning. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved)

item.title: Task-evoked pupillary responses reveal a role for attentional intensity in auditory discrimination.
item.content:encoded: Sensory discrimination has long been theorized to reflect a core cognitive function underlying intelligence. Building on this tradition, we examined whether task-evoked pupil responses, as an index of mental effort, relate to attention control (AC) and auditory discrimination ability. Using a large data set (N = 336), participants completed three adaptive auditory discrimination tasks (pitch, duration, loudness), a cognitive battery assessing AC, working memory capacity, and fluid intelligence, and pupillometry during task performance. Structural equation modeling confirmed that AC predicted auditory discrimination thresholds and fully mediated the relationship between task-evoked pupil dilation and performance. Trial-level multilevel models revealed that higher task difficulty and errors were associated with larger pupil dilations, especially in demanding tasks. Crucially, individuals with greater AC exhibited steeper increases in pupil dilation with rising task difficulty and were more resilient to performance declines. For high-AC individuals, large pupil responses predicted preserved accuracy; for low-AC individuals, they signaled compensatory effort with diminished success. These results suggest that AC governs both the extent and efficacy of mental effort, determining whether high arousal facilitates or fails to improve performance. This work refines classic resource models by demonstrating that cognitive effort, indexed via pupillometry, supports perception most effectively when guided by strong AC. Findings support a hierarchical model in which AC serves as the functional bridge between arousal, sensory discrimination, and higher order cognition.
